title: Java Runtime & Memory: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Night-before revision of the Java platform internals: JDK/JRE/JVM, bytecode and JIT, class loading, stack vs heap, garbage collection, String pool and immutability, and memory leaks.

chapters.title: JDK, JRE and JVM Mental Model
points: JVM: the virtual machine that loads and executes bytecode, and is platform-specific, while the bytecode stays platform-independent (write once, run anywhere)
JRE = JVM + core class libraries (java.lang, java.util...) needed to run programs; it has no compiler
JDK = JRE + dev tools (javac, jar, javadoc, jdb, jlink, jcmd); needed to develop
Containment: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM; since Java 11 Oracle ships no separate JRE (some vendors such as Eclipse Temurin still do), so use a JDK or a jlink-built runtime
Pipeline: Hello.java → javac → Hello.class (bytecode) → java launcher starts JVM → class loader → execution engine

chapters.title: Bytecode, JIT and Class Loading
points: Bytecode is the stack-based, platform-neutral instruction set in .class files; inspect it with javap -c ClassName
Execution engine starts by interpreting bytecode, then JIT-compiles hot methods (C1 quick, C2 optimizing; tiered compilation) to native code
JIT optimizations: inlining, escape analysis, dead-code elimination; the warm-up cost is why short benchmarks mislead (use JMH)
Class loader hierarchy: Bootstrap (core JDK classes) → Platform (formerly Extension) → Application (classpath); each loader delegates to its parent first
Parent delegation prevents user code from replacing java.lang.String; loading is lazy (on first use) and goes load → link (verify, prepare, resolve) → initialize (static blocks run)
ClassNotFoundException (checked, dynamic load failed, e.g. Class.forName) vs NoClassDefFoundError (error, class present at compile time but missing at runtime)

chapters.title: Stack vs Heap Memory
points: Stack: one per thread, holds frames (local variables, operand stack, return address); a frame is pushed per method call and popped on return
Heap: shared by all threads, holds all objects and arrays; managed by the garbage collector
Primitives locals live in the stack frame; for object locals the reference is on the stack and the object is on the heap; Java is always pass-by-value (the reference is copied)
Stack is fast, LIFO and freed automatically on return; heap is slower and reclaimed only by GC

StackOverflowError = too-deep or infinite recursion (tune with -Xss); OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space = heap exhausted (tune with -Xms/-Xmx); class metadata lives in Metaspace (native memory, since Java 8), while static fields live on the heap, held by the Class object

chapters.title: Garbage Collection Basics
points: An object is eligible for GC when no live GC root (thread stacks, static fields, JNI refs) can reach it; reference counting is not used, so cycles are collected
Generational heap: Young (Eden + Survivor S0/S1) and Old; most objects die young; survivors age and get promoted to Old after a threshold
Minor GC cleans Young (frequent, fast); Major/Full GC cleans Old (and more), is the slow one and can cause long stop-the-world pauses
Collectors: Serial (small apps), Parallel (throughput), G1 (default since Java 9, balanced low pause), ZGC/Shenandoah (very low pause, large heaps)
System.gc() is only a hint, not a guarantee, so avoid it; finalize() is deprecated, so use try-with-resources or Cleaner
Useful flags: -Xms/-Xmx heap size, -XX:+UseG1GC, -Xlog:gc for GC logs

chapters.title: String Pool and Immutability
points: String is immutable: its value cannot change after creation, and every 'modification' (concat, replace, toUpperCase) returns a new String
String pool: a cache of unique string literals inside the heap (since Java 7); literals with the same text share one object
String s = "hi" reuses or creates it in the pool; new String("hi") always creates a new heap object; intern() returns the pooled instance
"a" == "a" is true (same pooled object) but new String("a") == "a" is false; always compare content with equals(), never ==
Why immutable: safe pool sharing, thread safety, cached hashCode (safe HashMap keys), security for class names, paths and credentials
Concatenating in a loop creates many garbage objects: use StringBuilder (not thread-safe, fast) or StringBuffer (synchronized, slower)

chapters.title: Memory Leaks and Cheat Sheet
points: Java leak = objects still reachable but never used again, so GC cannot free them; it ends in OutOfMemoryError

Top causes: static collections that only grow, unclosed resources (streams, connections), listeners/callbacks never deregistered, ThreadLocal not removed in thread pools, bad equals/hashCode keys in HashMap
Diagnose: jps / jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info, jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>, then analyze with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM; add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
Fixes: try-with-resources, remove listeners, bounded caches or WeakHashMap, ThreadLocal.remove() in finally

Cheat sheet: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM; javac then java; javap -c bytecode; parent-delegation loaders; stack per thread vs shared heap; Young→Old generations, G1 default; equals() not ==; StringBuilder in loops; heap dump on OOM
